items.q: How much does software product development cost?
items.a: The cost varies depending on the scope, complexity, integrations, and expected scale of the product. There is a big difference between building an MVP and developing a full platform with multiple user roles and systems behind it. A custom software product development company usually defines the budget after a discovery phase, where requirements, risks, and priorities are clearly mapped.

items.q: How long does it take to build a software product?
items.a: There is no universal timeline. Some products can be launched in a few months as an MVP, while others require long-term development with multiple iterations. What matters more is how the process is structured and how quickly you can start validating your idea in the market.

items.q: What are the key stages of the software product development process?
items.a: It typically starts with discovery, where the idea is shaped into clear requirements. Then comes product design and architecture, followed by development and testing. After launch, the focus shifts to continuous improvement, scaling, and adding features based on user feedback.

items.q: What is MVP and Poс in software product development?
items.a: A PoC, or Proof of Concept, is created to validate whether a technical idea, feature, or solution is feasible before full product development begins. An MVP is a simplified version of a product that includes only core functionality. It is built to test the idea in real conditions, gather feedback, and understand what actually matters to users before investing in full development.

items.q: How do you ensure product-market fit and product success?
items.a: Product-market fit is not something you achieve once and move on. It is a continuous process of testing, learning, and adjusting. Teams that stay close to users, track behavior, and iterate quickly are the ones that build products people actually use.

items.q: Can you scale and improve a product after launch?
items.a: Yes, and in most cases that is when the real product work begins. After launch, teams focus on performance, infrastructure, and new features. Scaling is not only about technology but also about adapting the product to growing user needs and business goals.
